section_summary: This section contains State Department policy memoranda and diplomatic correspondence from November and December 1949 concerning the proposed Japanese peace treaty and the question of Japanese rearmament. It includes a memorandum from W. Walton Butterworth and John B. Howard to the Secretary of State, with an attached position paper, presenting political, constitutional, and diplomatic arguments against authorizing the reactivation of Japanese armed forces. In addition, it contains Despatch No. 329 from the American Embassy in Wellington transmitting and analyzing New Zealand press commentary that expressed apprehension over the revival of Japanese military power and warned against a new policy of appeasement.

subfiles.about: Memorandum and position paper setting forth the Department of State's opposition to authorizing the reactivation of Japanese armed forces in the proposed peace treaty.
subfiles.from: W. Walton Butterworth and John B. Howard
subfiles.summary: Director of Far Eastern Affairs Butterworth and Policy Planning Staff consultant Howard recommend submitting an attached position paper to the Department of Defense outlining the State Department's objections to authorizing the reactivation of Japanese armed forces in the proposed peace treaty. The attached paper sets forth six principal political and strategic reasons against Japanese rearmament, emphasizing Japan's constitutional renunciation of war, the priority of economic recovery, regional apprehensions among Pacific Allies, and the necessity of preventing armed conflict rather than preparing for defense against Soviet attack.
subfiles.title: Reactivation of Japanese Armed Forces

subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the Department of State memorandum and position paper regarding the non-reactivation of Japanese armed forces in the peace treaty.
subfiles.from: W. Walton Butterworth and John B. Howard
subfiles.summary: This is a duplicate carbon copy from the Special Files of the November 15, 1949 memorandum from Butterworth and Howard to the Secretary of State. It includes the accompanying November 16, 1949 position paper presenting the Department of State's detailed political and strategic arguments against authorizing Japanese armed forces in the peace treaty.
subfiles.title: Reactivation of Japanese Armed Forces

subfiles.about: Foreign Service despatch reporting New Zealand public anxiety over the possible rearmament of Japan and transmitting an article by 'Criticus'.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Scotten transmits and analyzes an article from the Wellington Labor weekly The Standard by 'Criticus' (W. Rosenberg) criticizing alleged U.S. appeasement of Japan. The despatch and attached article highlight widespread New Zealand anxiety that building up paramilitary police forces and rehabilitating conservative leaders could lead to a revival of Japanese militarism reminiscent of the 1938 Munich agreement.
subfiles.title: Rearmament of Japan

subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of a New Zealand press article warning against a new Munich policy through the remilitarization of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate copy of an article by 'Criticus' from The Standard arguing that expanding Japanese police forces and accommodating conservative politicians like Yoshida risks reviving Japanese militarism and repeating the errors of Munich appeasement.
subfiles.title: N.Z. Apprehensions Over Possible Rearmament of Japan: Beware of Munich
